course.title: Node js
course.description: A research-driven Node.js course progressing from runtime fundamentals to asynchronous programming, modules and npm, filesystem and streams, HTTP and networking, process concurrency, security, testing and diagnostics, production operations, and advanced integration. The curriculum teaches Node.js itself before frameworks and finishes with a realistic dependency-free incident journal service.
prerequisites: Basic JavaScript syntax, functions, objects, arrays, modules and promises.
Comfort with a terminal and editing files.
Basic HTTP and JSON familiarity is helpful but not mandatory.
learningOutcomes: Explain Node.js as a runtime and select supported release lines.
Design asynchronous programs with promises, cancellation and event-loop awareness.
Use ESM/CommonJS and npm package boundaries deliberately.
Implement filesystem, JSON persistence and streaming workflows safely.
Build HTTP servers and clients with validation, limits and lifecycle handling.
Use workers and child processes when isolation or CPU concurrency is required.
Apply secure configuration, cryptographic randomness, dependency hygiene and defense-in-depth permissions.
Write tests and investigate performance or operational failures using built-in diagnostics.
Design a maintainable Node service with explicit boundaries and graceful shutdown.

project.name: Incident Journal Service
project.description: A dependency-free incident journal HTTP service and CLI that integrates Node.js runtime, ESM, HTTP, URL parsing, filesystem persistence, cryptographic IDs, AsyncLocalStorage, configuration, testing, timeouts, and graceful shutdown.
steps: Create the project directories shown in the code map.
Run npm test.
Start the HTTP server with npm start.
Call GET /health.
POST an incident to /incidents.
Call GET /incidents.
Run the CLI list/count commands.
Send SIGINT or SIGTERM and inspect shutdown logs.
Review which layer would be replaced if JSON storage were replaced by a database.

code.src/service.js:
import {randomUUID} from 'node:crypto';
export function createIncidentService(store,now=()=>new Date().toISOString()){return {async list(){return store.load()},async create(input){if(!input||typeof input!=='object')throw new TypeError('body must be an object');if(typeof input.title!=='string'||input.title.trim().length<3)throw new Error('title must contain at least 3 characters');const items=await store.load();const incident={id:randomUUID(),title:input.title.trim(),severity:['low','medium','high','critical'].includes(input.severity)?input.severity:'medium',status:'open',createdAt:now()};items.push(incident);await store.save(items);return incident}}}

project.explanation: The HTTP layer owns protocol parsing and response formatting. The service owns incident validation and domain construction. The store owns JSON persistence and performs a complete temporary write before replacing the primary file. AsyncLocalStorage carries a request ID through asynchronous service work. randomUUID supplies an opaque identifier. The built-in test runner verifies service behavior in temporary directories. The server sets explicit request/header timeouts and handles SIGTERM/SIGINT through an idempotent, bounded shutdown path. The project is dependency-free to keep Node.js behavior visible; production deployments would add authentication/authorization, centralized observability, backup strategy, deployment-specific TLS/proxy configuration, and a durable multi-writer persistence layer when requirements demand them.
